paragraphs.text: Coastal towns face difficult choices as sea levels rise. Engineer Mark Doyle favours building higher sea walls, arguing that they have protected the Dutch coast for centuries and that the cost is small compared with the value of the property behind them.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Geographer Priya Nair disagrees. She points out that sea walls often increase erosion on nearby beaches, and she argues that in some places it would be wiser to allow the sea to flood low-lying farmland, creating salt marshes that absorb the energy of storms.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The Coastal Communities Group, which represents residents, accepts that some change is unavoidable but insists that no family should be forced to move without fair compensation. It has asked the government to publish long-term plans for each town.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Doyle admits that walls cannot be raised forever. He believes that within fifty years some towns will need to combine walls with natural defences, a view that Nair describes as a welcome step.
paragraphs.label: D
